questions.text: How do trace IDs and parent span IDs help diagnose latency across an agent, its tools, and remote calls?

options.A: They replace timing data with the order in which log lines were printed.
options.B: They group related operations and preserve their parent-child relationships.
options.C: They guarantee that every remote operation completes successfully.
options.D: They expose prompt contents automatically for every timed operation.

questions.explanation: A shared trace ID groups the operations; parent span IDs link their hierarchy so timings can be interpreted across agent, tool, and remote-call boundaries.

questions.text: You need latency and token-usage diagnostics, but prompts may contain private customer data. Which capture policy fits this lesson?

options.A: Record full prompts by default and remove trace identifiers.
options.B: Disable all tracing because timing requires prompt contents.
options.C: Capture every completion and trust the exporter to infer redactions.
options.D: Keep timing and usage metadata while leaving prompt/completion capture off unless explicitly approved.

questions.explanation: Operational timing and usage can be recorded without prompt or completion content. The lesson makes sensitive content capture opt-in.

questions.text: In agent_loop(), there is one root span, two LLM spans, and a loop over three cities that creates a tool span plus one MCP span per city. How many spans does one invocation append to an initially empty SPANS list?

options.D: 3 spans: 1 root + 2 LLM, since children are not appended.

questions.explanation: start_span appends every span. Each of three city iterations adds two spans, giving 1+2+3*2=9.
